content:
RESOLVED:
1.         That
this Council:
a)     
Agrees to the creation of an Active Travel
Councillor Champion role to sit alongside existing Councillor
Champion roles; and
b)    
Agrees the Draft Role profile attached and delegates
authority to the Director of Law and Governance to make minor
changes to the role profile.
c)     
Notes the delegation to the Director of Law and
Governance to make appointments to all 
Councillor Champion roles in consultation with the Leaders of
Political Groups, and looks forward to confirmation of appointments
in due course.
 

 

Annex
Milton Keynes City Council Active Travel Councillor Champion
Role Profile
The Post holder
·           
A serving MKCC Councillor nominated by the Leaders
of Political Groups who advocates for walking, wheeling and cycling
across Milton Keynes, promoting the benefits of active travel for
health, wellbeing, accessibility, sustainability and reducing
congestion and air pollution.
·           
Appointed by the Council to emphasise the importance
the Council places on the role.
The role
The Champion will assist the
Council, Leader and appropriate Cabinet Members to increase
opportunities for active travel, improve the redway network and
encourage more residents to choose sustainable forms of transport
for everyday journeys.
Responsibilities:
·           
Promote the benefits of walking, wheeling and
cycling across Milton Keynes.
·           
Act as a visible advocate for active travel within
the Council and across the city.
·           
Champion the needs of pedestrians, cyclists,
mobility scooter users and other active travel users.
·           
Support the Council’s ambitions to improve and
enhance the redway network and wider active travel
infrastructure.
·           
Engage with residents, community groups, schools,
businesses and partner organisations to encourage greater
participation in active travel.
·           
Raise awareness of active travel initiatives,
campaigns and events taking place across the city such as Love to
Ride, Bikeability and Festival of Cycling.
·           
Work collaboratively with the relevant Cabinet
Members, officers and stakeholders to support the delivery of the
Council Plan and transport strategies.
·           
Promote the links between active travel, public
health, environmental sustainability and community
wellbeing.
·           
Attend relevant meetings, events and stakeholder
meetings where appropriate.
·           
Help the council to identify opportunities and
barriers to increase active travel.
topline: The Milton Keynes City Council has decided to create an Active Travel Councillor Champion role to promote walking, wheeling, and cycling in the city.

content:
RESOLVED:

1.      This Council notes
that:
a)           
Nationally, around 1
in 5 children aged 8-16 are experiencing a probable mental health
disorder, with many difficulties emerging before secondary
school.
b)           
In Milton Keynes,
partners estimate that nearly 13,000 young people aged 8-25 are
living with a diagnosable mental health condition, placing
significant pressure on statutory services.
c)            
Local families report
long waiting times for mental health assessments through local GPs
and CAMHS, alongside high eligibility thresholds that leave many
children without support.
d)           
Children aged 8-12 can
wait months for an assessment and further months for outcomes,
during which time they often receive little or no interim support,
increasing the risk of escalating to crisis point.
e)           
Families navigating
neurodivergent assessment pathways often face complex and unclear
processes, with limited information on how to seek help.
f)             
The current Mental
Health Strategy is shared across Milton Keynes, Bedford and Luton,
which can limit the city’s ability to tailor provision to
suit local need.
g)           
CHUMS (Mental Health
& Emotional Wellbeing Service), funded by the Bedfordshire,
Luton and Milton Keynes Integrated Care Board (BLMK ICB[1]) with a
contribution from the City Council, provides early emotional
wellbeing and mental health support for children and young people
aged 7-18, offering an important opportunity to strengthen early
intervention locally.
2.            
This Council believes
that:
a)           
Early preventative
mental health support is more effective for children and families
and is better value for public money than reactive or crisis-led
support.
b)           
Children aged 8-12
face specific pressures, including academic expectations, family
instability, neurodiversity, the influence of social media, and
anxiety from the transition from primary to secondary
school.
c)            
No child should be
left without support while waiting for assessment where early help
could prevent deterioration.
d)           
Families should not
have to navigate complex systems to find help, clear, accessible
and locally tailored information is essential.
e)           
Milton Keynes should
maximise its influence within the shared mental health strategy to
better reflect the city’s rapid growth and demographic
pressures.
f)             
Effective partnership
working between CAMHS, CHUMS, schools, GPs, local charities and
Parish and Town Councils is essential to prevent children falling
through service gaps.
3.            
This Council resolves
to:
a)           
Request that the
Children and Young People Scrutiny Committee, working with
information provided by the Bedfordshire, Luton and Milton Keynes
Integrated Care Board (BLMK ICB) and relevant partners review
provision for children aged 8-12 including:
i)         
current
waiting times for assessments;
ii)       
referral
thresholds for support; and
iii)     
interim
support available to children while awaiting assessment.
b)           
Ask the Children and
Young People Scrutiny Committee to consider within its work
programme:
i)         
how short-term early
intervention sessions can be made more widely available while
children await assessment; and
ii)       
how services such as
CHUMS can be better aligned with CAMHS and GP referral pathways to
reduce gaps in support.
c)            
Request that the
Leader writes to the BLMK Integrated Care Board encouraging it to
explore external funding opportunities, including grants to expand
early intervention provision for children aged 8-12.
d)           
Improve publicly
accessible signposting, including clearer information on referral
pathways, neurodivergent assessment routes and voluntary sector
support available locally.
e)           
Engage with NHS
partners to ensure Milton Keynes specific needs are clearly
reflected within the shared BLMK Mental Health Strategy.
topline: The UK council has decided to improve mental health support for children aged 8-12 in Milton Keynes by reviewing current provision, enhancing early intervention, aligning services, exploring funding opportunities, and improving public information.

content:
RESOLVED:

1.      This Council
notes:

a)           
That statutory undertakers, including utility companies and
telecommunications providers, carry out essential works on the public highway under powers granted by
the New Roads and Street Works Act 1991 (NRSWA).

b)           
That the
Specification for the Reinstatement of Openings in Highways
(SROH) sets minimum national
standards for reinstatement, but these standards often allow for
patching and surface finishes that fall below the original quality
of the highway or footway.

c)            
That poor or
substandard reinstatements contribute to long-term deterioration,
increased maintenance costs, trip hazards for pedestrians, and
reduced public confidence in the management of local
highways.

d)           
That local authorities
have limited powers to enforce “like-for-like”
reinstatement under existing regulations, but can strengthen their
stance through improved inspection regimes, use of Section 72 of
NRSWA (defective reinstatements), and
enhanced local policy frameworks.

2.            
This Council
believes:

a)           
That residents, businesses, and road users deserve reinstated
roads and pavements that meet or exceed their original standard—not merely the national
minimum.

b)           
That statutory
undertakers should leave the highway in no worse condition than
they found it, and ideally restored to a uniform, structurally
sound, and visually consistent state.

c)            
That improved
consistency and quality would reduce long-term maintenance
liabilities and improve public safety and satisfaction.

3.            
This Council resolves
to request that the Cabinet Member considers:

a)           
Enhancing inspection
practices by:

i)              
investigating capacity
for increasing Section 72 inspections and enforcement on defective
reinstatements; and

ii)            
publishing an annual
public report on reinstatement quality and compliance.

b)           
Strengthening cost recovery by ensuring that all available
recovery powers for remedial works are utilised consistently.

c)            
Engaging with
statutory undertakers to:

i)              
promote best
practice;

ii)            
agree shared local
standards exceeding minimum national requirements; and

iii)          
develop a joint
approach to minimising disruption and
improving reinstatement outcomes.

d)           
Lobbying the UK
Government through our 3 MPs to:

i)              
Request powers to
adopt a strengthened local reinstatement policy, requiring
statutory undertakers to deliver:
?           
like-for-like surface
materials and finishes;
?           
full-width or
partial-width resurfacing where patching would undermine surface
quality;
?           
reinstatements aligned
with the highest relevant category within SROH standards; and
?           
aesthetic matching of
paving types, kerbs, and slabs wherever
used.
ii)       
Amend NRSWA and SROH to
require mandatory like-for-like reinstatement as
standard.
iii)     
Strengthen local
authority powers to refuse inadequate reinstatement
materials.
iv)     
Provide additional
funding to support expanded inspection and enforcement
capacity.
v)       
Increase fines
permitted by local authorities substantially and for the local
authority to retain 100% for road improvements and recovery of
enforcement costs.
topline: The Council has decided to push for higher standards in road and pavement reinstatements by statutory undertakers.

content:
RESOLVED:

1.      This Council notes
that:

a)           
Milton Keynes City
Council’s Adult Social Care services were ranked among the
top ten performing local authorities for the quality of care
provided following the recent inspection by the Care Quality
Commission (CQC);

b)           
home care workers
provide essential support to vulnerable residents, helping people
remain independent and reducing pressure on hospitals;

c)            
travel time between
visits is a recognised challenge within the sector and can impact
workforce stability and continuity of care for residents;

d)           
the UNISON Ethical Care Charter states that home care workers
should be paid for their travel time, travel costs and other
necessary expenses such as mobile phones; and

e)           
Milton Keynes City
Council’s commissioning terms and conditions require home
care providers delivering services on behalf of the Council to
reflect the provisions of the UNISON Ethical Care
Charter.
2.            
This Council believes
that:

a)           
maintaining
high-quality care standards requires a fairly treated and properly
supported workforce; and

b)           
supporting professional development and recognised
qualifications for care workers can strengthen recruitment,
retention and quality of care provided.
3.            
This Council resolves
to ask that:

a)           
the Housing, Health and Adults Scrutiny Committee, as part of
its work programme, consider an item about how travel time and travel
costs are treated within commissioned home care contracts and how
providers demonstrate compliance with the Council’s
commissioning standards; and

b)           
the Executive to
explore how the Council can support professional development and
recognised qualifications for care workers in Milton Keynes to
improve retention, quality of care and to maintain high standards
of care.
topline: The Council has decided to address travel time and travel costs for home care workers in Milton Keynes, as well as support professional development and qualifications for care workers.

content:
The Head of Economic Growth and Inward Investment (West
Northamptonshire Council) outlined that an opportunity had arisen
to bid for Local Innovation Partnership funding. Nationally, a pot
of £500 million had been made available to support local
innovation partnerships based on a “triple helix” model
bringing together local authorities, businesses and universities.
It was noted that the fund was highly competitive, with an
expectation that only around six bids nationally would be
successful. Partners had worked together to develop a single, inter
dependent portfolio of projects, built around the concept of an
“innovation circuit” within the region. This concept
involved linking some of the strongest assets in the area,
recognizing: existing strengths in motorsport engineering and
design; advanced manufacturing capabilities; connected and
autonomous systems; smart city technologies; and space science and
engineering. These sectoral and spatial strengths would be
underpinned by the capabilities of local universities.
The Executive Director for Place and Economy (North
Northamptonshire Council) noted support for the project and that
North Northamptonshire Council was very keen to work with the
project leads and highlighted the opportunity for a “ripple
effect” of benefits across the wider South Midlands
region.
The Chief Executive of Bedford Borough Council noted that
the bid was very good but challenged whether the collaborative bid
would still have come together without the existence of the South
Midlands Authorities structure. It was further noted that future
papers should be clearer on what additional contribution and
facilitation the South Midlands team brought to such
bids.
The Chair highlighted that collaboration would always take
place across different footprints and the strength of this bid was
that it encompassed not only Bedford, Luton and Milton Keynes
(BLMK) and the Northamptonshire areas, but also Buckinghamshire. It
was further noted that regardless of where areas ended up in terms
of devolution, there would always be a need to work constructively
with adjoining areas such as Buckinghamshire, Cambridgeshire and
Peterborough, and Oxfordshire.
The Executive Director, Place, Economy and Environment
(West Northamptonshire Council) endorsed the value added by the
South Midlands Authorities (SMAB) and suggested that its role was
in enabling collaboration rather than silo working; and the SMAB
therefore helped to frame those conversations and provide a central
mechanism for taking work forward.
RESOLVED:
That the
Board note the update in the report.
topline: The West Northamptonshire Council has decided to bid for Local Innovation Partnership funding to support regional innovation partnerships.

content:
N Butters, Vice Chair of the
South Midlands Business Board reminded members that the SMAB had
not endorsed the South Midlands Economic Growth Strategy at their
last meeting and that the Business Board were proposing the
following options to progress the strategy:
·           
Cosmetic/superficial changes (Option 1)
·           
Light touch refresh of existing draft (Option
2)
·           
Enhanced economic baseline report (Option
3)
It was noted by members that
there were other sectors and issues that had been raised at the
previous meeting which did not appear to be addressed by this
report.
The Chair indicated that having
discussed the matter with Councillor Simmons that neither Milton
Keynes or Luton could support the strategy as currently written
without clear caveats and incorporating the previous feedback that
had been made. It was reiterated that their position was that
Northamptonshire and BLMK were discrete areas with overlap, which
the report did not reflect. The Chair expressed his concern that
the Business Board appeared to be intent on creating a baseline for
a single economic area, which was not the direction the Board had
been given.
The Chair proposed that any
decision for additional funding for further work on the strategy
must be provisional on the Business Board providing a clear
explanation as to how the strategy would be future?proofed in case
the South Midlands area did not continue as one area as a result of
devolution. The Chair stressed that the Business Board was a
sub-board who advised the SMAB and must therefore take the politics
of the situation into account and that the strategy must be
devolution?proof.
Councillor Baker placed on
record that Central Bedfordshire Council had recently debated the
matter and had passed a motion confirming it was not wedded to the
BLMK area and was exploring all potential options.
The Vice Chair of the Business
Board noted that businesses on the Board wanted to work
collaboratively and that a strengthened strategy would bring
opportunities across the South Midlands. She undertook to relay the
points raised back to the Board.
The Chair asked Councillor Weir
to relay to the Business Board Chair that while constructive
disagreement on devolution footprints was acceptable, it was not
acceptable for the Business Board’s leadership to pursue a
single approach contrary to the collective view of the South
Midlands Authorities Board.
Councillor Weir indicated that
future?proofing the strategy was essential and that he supported
developing a dual?function approach within the economic strategy
that could separate the two geographies if necessary, so that the
Board could move forward pragmatically whatever the outcome on
devolution.
The Executive Director of
Place, Economy and Environment (West Northamptonshire Council)
sought clarification on timing of the assurances that had been
requested and the Chair advised that this should be provided as
soon as possible, via email to the members of the South Midlands
Authorities Board. It was further noted that beyond a paper
assurance to unlock funding, the SMAB needed confidence that the
approach would be carried through in delivery.
RESOLVED:
That the
Board:
a)            
Noted the update in this
report;
b)           
Approved Option 3 as the
preferred approach, funded from South Midlands reserves and
endorsed by the South Midlands Business Board as the option most
capable of delivering the robust, evidence led strategy required;
and
c)            
Noted that approval of (b) and
release of funding, is conditional on the South Midlands
Authorities Board members receiving written assurance from the
Chair of the South Midlands Business Board to demonstrate that the strategy would be developed on a dual?model
basis rather than a single South Midlands model, and how it would
be future?proofed against different devolution outcomes.
topline: The South Midlands Authorities Board has decided to approve Option 3 for the Economic Growth Strategy, with funding conditional on future-proofing against devolution outcomes.

content:
The Head of Economic Growth and
Inward Investment (West Northamptonshire Council) introduced the
report setting out the context and options for the use of reserves
held on behalf of the South Midlands Authorities. Members were
reminded that, when the services transferred in April 2020, the
Accountable Body had operated a £1.0m contingency to
safeguard against financial, operational and legacy liabilities.
Following reassessment, the Accountable Body recommended that it
would be prudent that the contingency be increased to
£1.5m.
The report also considered
three main options for the use of available reserves which were:
Option 1 - Targeted Investment in Regional Projects and
Programmes; Option 2a -
Shared Allocation Between Local Authorities and South Midlands
Services; Option 2b - Allocation to Local Authorities
Only; Option 3 - Retain Reserves for Long Term Strategic
Purposes.
The report confirmed that in
addition to the contingency, a £300k service risk reserve and
£1.3m ring?fenced grant fund would remain ring?fenced and
were not available for allocation under Option 2a or 2b.
The Chair confirmed that, due
to existing motions at Milton Keynes City Council and Luton Borough
Council, a joint committee could not be established, and decisions
would therefore need to proceed through each authority’s own
governance processes.
Councillor Weir proposed that
the Board accept Option 2b which was seconded by Councillor Marland
and supported by the remaining leaders. Councillor Marland proposed
that this was an even split between the six authorities which was
seconded by Councillor Weir and agreed by the remaining
leaders.
Councillor Baker asked for
clarification on the proposed £1.5m contingency and for the
workings behind the revised figures. Officers indicated some of the
changes that had led to this increase and members were reminded
that the inter?authority agreement envisaged joint responsibility
if liabilities exceeded available reserves and this recommendation
sought to avoid that situation. It was proposed that the detailed
workings of what made up the contingency fund be made available to
the Chair and Vice Chair for assurance and transparency.
The Chief Executive of Milton
Keynes Council supported a simple, non?bureaucratic distribution of
the reserves and asked officers to advise on the simplest method so
that relatively modest sums were not delayed by lengthy decision
cycles or dependency on each authority’s governance
timetable. Officers noted that the host authority would implement
whatever the Board decided with regard to distributing the funds
and that each authority would need to be content with their
internal delegations to achieve this.
It was noted that the report
referred to an outstanding loan that was the responsibility of
North Northamptonshire Council and a report on this would be
brought to the next Board meeting.
The Chair acknowledged the work
of the team at West Northamptonshire for driving down costs over
the past 18 months and dealing with the legacy overspend of the
former LEP, which, as a company, had not been required to balance
its budget in the way public bodies must.
The Chair confirmed there was
no dissent from members with agreeing Option 2b and summarised that
decision?making to return the funds would sit with each individual
authority.
RESOLVED:
That the
Board:

a)            
Noted the update in this paper
and the current position of South Midlands reserves.

b)           
Agreed that there would be no
changes to the current governance arrangements for the South
Midlands Authorities Board.

c)            
Agreed that £1.5m
contingency be retained by the South Midlands Authorities and held
on their behalf by the Accountable Body, West Northamptonshire
Council subject to the Accountable Body providing the Chair and
Vice Chair of the South Midlands Authorities Board with the
detailed workings behind the £1.5m.

d)           
Agreed that the remaining South
Midlands reserves would be split equally between the six
authorities and that the Accountable Body would distribute the
funds to each authority on receipt of any individual governance
approvals that were required.

e)           
Noted that North
Northamptonshire Council would provide a report for the next
meeting on the outstanding loan to Corby Electric.
At the
conclusion of the meeting members placed on
record their thanks to the Chair for his longstanding leadership of
the Board and service to the area. The Chair acknowledged the
comments and also commended Councillor Simmons for her long service
in Luton and wished the Board well for the future.
 
The
Chair closed the meeting at 10.51 am.
topline: The West Northamptonshire Council has decided to retain a £1.5m contingency for South Midlands Authorities and split the remaining reserves equally among the six authorities.

content:
1.         That
condition 2.3 be removed in its entirety and replaced
with:

           
‘That one SIA licensed door supervisor be on duty at the
premises from
21:00 hours on Fridays, Saturdays and Bank Holidays when open until
the premises closes to the public’.

2.         That
there be a designated smoking area at the front of the premises
only.

3.         That the
following conditions be added to the current licence:

(a)        An adequate
CCTV system shall be installed, maintained and operated at the
premises before any licensable activities may take place and
thereafter. The CCTV system shall cover all licensed areas inside
and all entrances and exits. The system shall record continuously
whilst the premises are open to the public and for licensable
activities. Images must be of an evidentiary standard and be date
and time stamped. The system installed must retain all images for a
minimum of 31 days and these must be made available for the Local
Authority, the Licensing Authority or the Police to view or remove
on request. A member of staff trained in working the system and
capable of downloading images shall be on duty whenever the
premises are open to the public.

(b)       An effective
Challenge 25 policy shall be implemented and maintained in place at
the premises. Any persons appearing to be under the age of 25 who
attempts to purchase alcohol must be challenged in respect of their
age and required to provide adequate proof that they are over the
age of 18 before they are sold or supplied with alcohol.

(c)        Each member of
staff involved in alcohol sales will receive adequate training in
the law with regard to alcohol sales and a written record of the
training each person has received shall be maintained. Regular
refresher training will also be given and recorded. The training
records / logs are to be kept on site / electronically or at Head
Office and shall be provided to the Local Authority, the Licensing
Authority or the Police upon request.

(d)       Only photographic
based forms of identification shall be accepted as proof of age in
respect of suspected underage sales. These must be accredited to
the PASS scheme or subsequent equivalent but could also include
passport, HM forces ID card, and driving licence.

(e)        A refusal log
/ form to record all attempts to purchase alcohol that were refused
shall be kept on site and all refused sales recorded. The log shall
be provided to the Local Authority, the Licensing Authority or the
Police upon request.

(f)        An incident
log shall be maintained and kept at the premises, and made
available on request to the Local Authority, the Licensing
Authority or the Police, which will record the
following:

(i)         all
crimes which occur within the venue;

(ii         all
ejections of patrons;

(iii)       any incidents of
disorder;

(iv)       seizures of drugs or
offensive weapons; and

(v)        any refusals
of the sale of alcohol.

(g)        The Premises
Licence Holder shall ensure that all staff working at the premises
shall undertake vulnerable persons / child awareness training, this
training shall incorporate vulnerable person / child exploitation
awareness and what steps to undertake where necessary.

(h)       Off sales of alcohol
shall be in sealed containers from 23:00 hours.

(i)         Except
for exceptional circumstances the Designated Premises Supervisor or
another Personal Licence Holder will be on duty at the premises on
Friday and Saturday evenings and Bank Holidays from 21:00 hours
until the premises close to the public.


 

(j)         Where
the licensee employs / engages any person at or about the premises
in the capacity of a door supervisor, the licensee shall maintain a
register which shall be kept at the premises for a period of at
least twelve months. The register shall note the name, licence
number of any door supervisors employed with the dates and times
they worked and be produced for inspection by the Local Authority,
the Licensing Authority or the Police upon request.

(k)        The premises
shall implement a customer dispersal policy to assist with
minimising noise disturbance to local residents from
customers leaving the premises.  Notices
shall be prominently displayed at all public exits requesting
customers to respect the needs of local residents and leave the
premises and area quietly.

(l)         Doors
and windows are to be closed except for access and egress
after
23:00 hours.

(m)      A dedicated telephone
number for the premises must be given to any resident upon request
to allow complaints to be made directly at all times the premises
are open.

(n)       A complaints log
will be maintained and all complaints from residents will be
recorded therein.  Any complaint logged
will include date, time, name of complainant (if known) and reason
for complaint.  Any action taken in
relation to that complaint to also be recorded.  A copy of the log will be made available to
officers of the the Local Authority, the Licensing Authority or the Police
upon request.
topline: The Licensing Sub Committee has decided to approve recommendations for changes to a premises licence, including strict requirements for CCTV, staff training, and customer dispersal policy.

content:
RESOLVED:

1.     
This Council notes:

a)     
That residents can feel unsafe when long stretches of grid roads,
including roundabouts, bridges and busy junctions, are left without
functioning streetlights. Whilst some of these areas benefit
from basic lighting from nearby buildings or roadside lighting,
some are obscured by trees and remain in complete darkness. These
locations include various areas across the city, and the list has
been forwarded to the relevant Cabinet Member.

b)     
That residents walking or cycling along redways are also at risk from widespread outages,
particularly at busy junctions. Cyclists and pedestrians often
have to share narrow pathways, which are
frequently covered by debris or slippery leaves, all of which pose
additional hazards in poor lighting.

c)     
Accidents that involve vehicles and pedestrians and/or cyclists are
proportionally more likely to result in casualties and/or
fatalities. Due to financial constraints, the City Council
prioritise grid roads with the highest repair priority and
redways and underpasses are among the
lowest.

d)     
That given the number of redways and
underpasses with streetlights across the city, which is a very
large network to maintain, some of these routes can be left in
darkness for extended periods of time.

e)     
That these conditions can discourage active travel, as residents
are understandably reluctant to walk or cycle during the darker
months.

f)       That both councillors and
residents have expressed frustration at the difficulty of obtaining
clear updates on the causes and timescales of long running
faults.

2.     
This Council further notes:

a)     
That many streetlight repairs depend on National Grid,
and that close collaboration is essential to reduce delays and
improve safety.

b)     
The lack of clear information often leads to residents to believe
the City Council is solely responsible, which can be damaging to
its reputation.

3.     
This Council therefore asks:

a)     
The Executive to continue to engage proactively with National Grid
to minimise delays to streetlight repairs and to
establish a clear and regular communication process so that
councillors and residents can receive timely updates and
explanations for prolonged faults.

b)     
The Environment and Place Scrutiny Committee to consider, as part
of its work programme, the current prioritisation process
for streetlight repairs with a focus on resident and
community safety.
topline: The Council has decided to improve communication and collaboration with National Grid for streetlight repairs to enhance safety for residents walking and cycling in poorly lit areas.

This Council, while noting that it is entirely a matter for the OU,
regrets the University's reported decision not to give further consideration to the possibility of a
city-centre campus for face-to-face teaching.

2.      The Council requests the
Cabinet review any impact this might have on the reinvigoration of
CMK; and the implications for city-centre in-person undergraduate
education, as referenced in the recent New Towns task force
report.

3.      While recognising that

Council remains committed to the provision of face-to-face
education at Levels 4 and above, having regard to the city's own
demographic profile, the increased number of students studying
where they live, and the move towards accelerated two year degrees.

4.      The Council notes the

University, Cranfield University offering degree apprenticeships,
Milton Keynes College offering foundation degrees, the University
of Buckingham providing the clinical element of its MBBS degree
through the University Hospital and the Milton Keynes campus of the
University of Bedfordshire.

5.      The Council requests the
Cabinet to discuss inviting these universities and college to a
conference at which the city's future post-secondary educational
provision might be considered.  Representatives of the city's
secondary schools might also be invited as well as of the Oxford
Cambridge Arc Universities Group, and of the Government.

content:
RESOLVED:

1.      This Council notes that:

a)           
Milton Keynes City Council, its members and staff
works in the public interest and is
entrusted with significant responsibility and authority by the
residents it serves.

b)           
All councillors are required to uphold the Nolan
Principles of Public Life, including integrity, accountability,
leadership and respect, which exist to maintain public confidence
in democratic institutions.

c)            
The occasional conduct of some councillors has
raised concern among residents about the tone and standards of
behaviour demonstrated in formal council settings, particularly in
interactions involving members of the public.

d)           
The promotion of high standards in public life is a
shared responsibility of all councillors, supported by the
Standards Committee and statutory officers, and is essential to
maintaining public confidence in the Council’s Code of
Conduct and its democratic processes.

e)           
Senior leadership roles within the Council carry an
enhanced responsibility to model appropriate conduct and set the
standard for others.

2.      This Council believes
that:

a)           
Civility and respectful conduct are not optional or
secondary considerations, but fundamental to effective local
democracy and public trust.

b)           
The way councillors speak to and about members of
the public matters and can either encourage or deter future civic
participation, including the engagement of young people and members
of the Youth Council.

c)            
Apologies are important in acknowledging harm
caused, but maintaining high standards in public life requires
consistent enforcement of expected behaviour across the whole
Council with everyone being treated equally

d)           
If local government is to attract and retain people
of integrity to stand for public office, and to maintain the trust
placed in elected representatives by residents, it must demonstrate
that the principles it promotes are actively upheld in
practice.

e)      Standards in public life
apply not only to how councillors behave in meetings or in direct
interactions with the public, but also to how they communicate with
residents more broadly and inaccuracies in that communication
undermine public trust, damage confidence in democratic
institutions and make it harder for residents to engage
meaningfully in local decision-making.

3.      This Council resolves
to:

a)           
Reaffirm its collective commitment to the Nolan
Principles of Public Life, with explicit emphasis on leadership,
respect and accountability in all interactions with members of the
public.

b)           
Set a clear expectation that all councillors,
regardless of seniority, conduct themselves respectfully in formal
and informal council settings, including meetings, committees,
public forums and consultations, especially when interacting with
members of the public.

c)            
Recognise the particular importance of appropriate
conduct towards young people, and the need to ensure that Council
spaces remain welcoming, safe and inclusive for all who engage in
democratic processes.

d)           
Affirm that any public communications in their
official capacity including leaflets, newsletters, emails, social
media posts and other forms of engagement should be accurate,
evidence based and verifiable facts and information in order to maintain public trust and
confidence.

e)      Request that the
Monitoring Officer and Democratic Services arrange a mandatory
refresher session for all councillors on the Code of Conduct after
local elections take place in May, with specific focus
on:

i)              
Power imbalance and public accountability

ii)            
Managing challenge and disagreement
appropriately

iii)          
Upholding standards in high-pressure or contentious
situations

f)       Commit to promoting
a culture of civility and mutual respect across the Council, so
that Milton Keynes City Council continues to be seen as a body that
leads by example and values public engagement.
topline: The Council has decided to reaffirm its commitment to high standards of conduct and communication by councillors in Milton Keynes City Council.

purpose:
To consider amending the Taxi Policy to allow
new applicants to be granted a licence with up to 11 DVLA
points.
content:
That
the Executive amend the Taxi Policy to state:

(a)        new applicants
be permitted to apply for a hackney carriage / private hire driver
licence as long as they have held a current DVLA licence for at
least 12 months and have no more than 11 DVLA points.  The applicant must successfully complete, amongst
other things, an approved practical driving course and the
Council’s driver assessment testing before they can be
granted a licence;

(b)       should an existing
licence holder receive a fixed penalty notice during the life of
their licence and have accrued between 9 - 11 DVLA points then they
must, once again, complete an approved
Council practical driving course at their own
expense.  Should an existing licence
holder go to 12 or more DVLA points then their Hackney Carriage /
Private Hire driver licence will be revoked, and they cannot
reapply until they have fewer than 12 DVLA points;[1]

(c)        should an
existing licence holder accrue further DVLA points (but remain 11
or fewer), after completing two approved
practical driving courses, then their Hackney
Carriage / Private Hire driver licence will be reviewed with a view
to: 

(i)        
completing the Council’s enhanced driver assessment test at
their own expense;

(ii)        taking an
alternative bespoke training/rehabilitation course(s) identified by
council officers at the driver’s own expense; and /
or

(iii)       being suspended for
up to 21 days.
topline: The Delegated Decisions has decided to amend the Taxi Policy to set criteria for new applicants and existing license holders regarding DVLA points and driving courses.

content:
The Sub-Committee noted the
Applicant’s Agent’s submission that the applicant had
invested in the premises and had vast experience in running
businesses; and there had been no evidence to support that the
licence would undermine the Licensing Objectives.
The Applicant had understood
the representations submitted from Trading Standards and Thames
Valley Police, as Responsible Authorities, and had agreed the
following conditions which, as a result, the representations had
been withdrawn:
Trading Standards

1.         The
premises licence holder will ensure that all delivery couriers
employed directly by the licence holder will be trained to ask any
customer to whom alcohol is delivered, who appears to be under the
age of 25 years to produce, before being sold alcohol,
identification being a passport or photocard driving licence
bearing a holographic mark or other form of identification that
complies with any mandatory condition that may apply to this
licence.

2.         The
premises licence holder will further ensure that the age
verification policy will apply whereby all 3rd party courier
contractors will ensure that couriers will be trained to ask any
customer to whom alcohol is delivered, who appears to be under the
age of 25 years to produce, before being sold alcohol,
identification being a passport or photocard driving licence
bearing a holographic mark or other form of identification that
complies with any mandatory condition that may apply to this
licence.

3.         Delivery
of alcohol shall be to a residential address or place of work
specified in the customer order.  The
delivery of alcohol must be by way of handed over to the customer
who ordered.
Thames Valley Police

1.         An
effective ‘Challenge 25 Policy' shall be implemented and
maintained in respect of all supply and delivery of alcohol. This
will require persons appearing to be under the age of 25 who
attempt to purchase alcohol being challenged in respect of their
age and required to provide adequate proof of age that they are
over the age of 18 before they are given alcohol via delivery or
when ordering on line.

2.         Where
third party carriers are used for deliveries, the contract shall
specify that they must comply effectively with the Challenge 25
policy. This will include that if any receiver of goods fails to
produce appropriate ID in respect of Challenge 25 then the delivery
will not be made.

3.         All
deliveries of alcohol must be to a residential or business address
and only be given to a person who is 18 years old or older. Alcohol
shall not be delivered to a public place i.e., in a street or park
etc.

4.         Only
photographic based forms of identification shall be accepted as
proof of age in respect of suspected under age sales. These must be
accredited to the PASS scheme or subsequent equivalent but could
also include passport, HM forces ID card, driving
licence.

5.         Each
member of staff involved in alcohol sales will receive adequate
training on the law with regard to alcohol sales and a written
record of the training each person has received shall be
maintained.  Regular refresher training
will also be given and recorded. The training records/logs are to
be kept on site / electronically or at Head Office and shall be
provided to the Police, the Local Authority or Licensing Authority
upon request.

6.         An
adequate CCTV system shall be installed, maintained and operated at
the premises. The CCTV system shall cover all licensed areas. The
system shall record continuously whilst the premises is open to the
public. Images must be of an evidentiary standard and be date and
time stamped. The system installed must retain all images for a
minimum of 30 days and these must be made available for the Police
or Licensing Authority to view or remove on request.
Environmental Health, as a
Responsible Authority, submitted a representation which primarily
related to noise disturbance and had requested the premises close
at 21:00 hours and there be no activity at the premises after 23:00
hours, which had been rejected by the Applicant.
The Sub-Committee noted the
representations from three residents which primarily related
to concerns around public nuisance; crime and disorder; and public
safety, particularly in connection with the proposed late-night
operation and the premises’ proximity to residential
properties. 
It was noted that the premises
was located on Simpson Road which comprised of residential
properties and small commercial units, and was positioned to the
main high street in Fenny Stratford, where several other licensed

content:
The
Director of Children’s Services introduced the report on the
Focused 40 initiative, informing the Partnership that the
Integrated Care Board and the four local authorities in Bedford,
Luton and Milton Keynes had worked together to identify 10 children
within each local authority area who were most impacted by
childhood trauma but did not qualify for support under the Mental
Health Act 1983 or meet the criteria for Continuing Health
Care.
The
Partnership heard that the initiative, which had been running for a
year, aimed to provide a new approach for these children who were
considered at high risk of harm either to themselves or others but
were struggling to access appropriate support and
provision.
Focusing
on the 10 children selected within Milton Keynes the Partnership
heard that outcomes had significantly improved over the course of
the initiative with much lower levels of risk observed and better
attendance of school, relationships with family etc. The Director
of Children’s Services highlighted that the success of the
scheme at present was predominantly due to the work of the Interim
Deputy Chief Nurse and the Assistant Director of Children’s
Social Care and that consideration would need to be given as to how
this could be made systemic so that more children could benefit
from the approach.
Members of
the Partnership expressed support for the approach, noting that the
initiative gave a compelling case that this would not only be
beneficial for outcomes for the children but also financially as
placement costs had reduced as a result of the focused support. The Director of
Children’s Services added that there were a number of children in residential care that would
benefit from this type of intervention although it would be quite
difficult to quantify costs to provide this. It was also
acknowledged that this was an excellent example of the benefits of
close partnership working between the ICB and the
Council.
RESOLVED
–
That the
report be noted.
topline: The Director of Children’s Services has decided to approve recommendations for the Focused 40 initiative to support children impacted by childhood trauma.

content:
The
Director of Neighbourhood Health,
Places and Partnerships introduced the Integrated Care Board (ICB)
Update report, highlighting that all ICBs had been asked to cut
running costs by 50% and that this had led to BLMK ICB agreeing to
work in a cluster formation with Cambridgeshire and Peterborough
ICB and Hertfordshire and West Essex ICB towards becoming a new
organization, the Central East ICB. She added that recruitment had
been undertaken for the new executive team which was now working
across the three current ICBs and a staff consultation had
commenced with a view to implementing as many changes as possible
during the current financial year.
The
Partnership heard that governance arrangements for the Central East
ICB had been revised which had led to the creation of a
neighbourhood health delivery committee
for Bedford, Luton and Milton Keynes which would be chaired by the
Chief Executive of Milton Keynes City Council. The Director of
Neighbourhood Health, Places and
Partnerships advised that this committee would be developing the
Neighbourhood Health Plan, for which a
draft plan must be completed by April 2026.
The
progress on the Community and Mental Health Transformation
Programme was also noted. The Partnership heard that the Case for
Change was signed off in September and the transformation
priorities had also been agreed but work was underway to consider
the community and mental health services across the Central East
footprint to inform the outcomes framework and revised
specifications.
At the
Milton Keynes level, the Partnership were informed that work had
been carried out with primary care networks to ensure that the
neighbourhood footprints aligned as
closely as possible with primary care network footprints to support
the neighbourhood working.
Members of
the Partnership expressed that there were many good examples of
neighbourhood working in Milton Keynes
such as the work of the Bletchley Pathfinder with schools to
provide expert guidance and practical advice for supporting
children within school settings.
It was
acknowledged that it was challenging to create footprints that
worked well across a number of organisations such as the primary care networks,
hospital and council but the current proposal would be reviewed to
see how effective it was. The Partnership heard that residents had
been interested in the work and the impact it would have on
services and work was underway to communicate effectively with
community groups and residents about what this meant.
Following
a question, the Director of Neighbourhood Health, Places and Partnerships
clarified that CNWL were one of the NHS Trust representatives on
the Neighbourhood Health Delivery
Committee.
RESOLVED
–
That the
report be noted.
topline: The Health & Care Partnership has decided to approve the restructuring of the Integrated Care Board into the Central East ICB and the development of a Neighbourhood Health Plan.

content:
As part of
the introduction to this item the Chair invited the Creative and
Cultural Manager to provide a definition of “culture.”
Officers explained that, following Department of Culture Media and
Sports and Arts Council England usage, culture encompassed arts,
heritage and creativity in all forms (theatre, music, dance, visual
arts, libraries, crafts, digital, etc.), delivered in both formal
and community settings and public realm.
The Chair
asked officers how the definition of culture and the strategy itself would capture the wide range of
cultures and heritage of those living in Milton Keynes so that it
reflected an international perspective and officers indicated that
the new strategy would clearly state ambitions and reflect
diversity.
A member
of the committee raised the following points: there seemed to be a
timing gap with the end of the current strategy and the start of
the new one; major infrastructure such as the events venue;
Universal Studios, East West Rail, OxCam Arc appeared to be omitted; were the needs
for various types of creative spaces being considered as well as
better support for the High Street; stronger inclusion of rural
villages was needed; and clarity was needed on partnerships and the
approach to delivery and investment. Officers clarified that the
papers circulated to the committee contained suggested priorities
to test with members and it was not the final draft strategy. The
work on the Cultural Infrastructure Plan (CIP) was outlined which
covered consumption spaces (theatres, music, comedy) and production
spaces (film/music studios, artists’ studios). The strong
joint working with the Economic Development team and Destination MK
was noted which aimed to maximise
visitor flows, including Universal visitors. Officers framed Milton
Keynes as a mix of “the new and the old” with museums
telling both ancient and new town stories and that the strategy
delivery would include stakeholders’ roles, KPIs, collaboration and monitoring and Milton
Keynes’ good position to leverage Arts Council England and
National Lottery Heritage Funding (NLHF). Officers noted that the timing of the
strategy was to allow for a more visible launch in 2027 for MK60
events and that the post?COVID priorities had been extended to
carry through to 2027.
A
committee member sought clarity on the timeframe and emphasised the
importance of sustainable funding being at the forefront, including
government and third sector sources. Officers noted they intended
to share a draft strategy at the end of January and to seek formal
adoption by the end of March. With regard
to funding: diversification; helping partners unlock funds;
and exploring a private?sector endowment for MK60 were
highlighted.
A member
suggested involving the Living Archive and highlighted some
examples of grassroots venues and artists needing recognition and
partnership. Officers noted support for the Living
Archive.
A
committee member asked if there was any baseline participation
data, what was the extent of rural inclusion in cultural
activities, costings for a city centre cultural hub and digital
mapping and improving communications so that residents knew about
events. Officers confirmed that baseline audience data was
collected annually from funded organisations and via Audience Agency and indicated
the inclusion of baselines and trajectories in the strategy. The
need for a rural focus was acknowledged as well as a communication
reliance on visitor?facing Destination Milton Keynes website. An
example was suggested of potentially delivering printed material to
new homes.
A
committee member encouraged embracing MK Heritage touchpoints such
as The Point and learning from Rugby Borough’s “Love
Rugby” campaign. Officers agreed noting that MK60 should be
an accessible neighbourhood focused
activity.
A member
noted the potential use of Milton Keynes Railway Station and other
city assets for creative advertising, including digital screens and
billboards and officers indicated that there were discussions being
held regarding use of physical assets for evergreen content and
event?specific digital messaging.
A
committee member stressed the costs and the need for a clear
private?sector offering and asked about the consultation scope and
whether the committee would see the draft. Officers indicated that
they were aiming to consult on the strategy early in the new year
and that while the timing might prevent it being considered by the
committee, members could respond to any consultation as an
individual.
A member
urged that all schools should be involved in MK60 and for a Culture
Day to be held in every school. Officers agreed and referenced a
recent workshop held in a school, the need to adapt to the capacity
of individual schools and the Youth Council’s campaign to
‘expanding, improving and setting
"Cultures Day" as a standard across schools in Milton
Keynes.’
A Ward
Councillor in attendance commented on the city centre public realm,
gloomy walkways, and wayfinding gaps to key venues and urged the
strategy to feed substantively into MK2050 and be seen as core, not
peripheral.
The Chair
highlighted supplementary schools and their role in sustaining
language and culture and challenged the “straitjacket”
of s106 being interpreted too narrowly for public art, seeking more
flexible application to culture.
RESOLVED:

1.            
The Committee noted the draft emerging priorities
for the Creative and Cultural Strategy 2027 - 2035.

2.            
That the Director of Planning and Placemaking
be asked to consider including the
following points in the draft strategy or other relevant
documents:
a)       
Within the strategy include a clear definition of
“Culture,” identify Milton Keynes’ unique selling
points (USP’s) and incorporate KPI’s and baseline data to ensure progress
can be measured.
b)      
Ensure plans to develop cultural infrastructure
accounts for both delivery and production spaces.
c)       
Improve wayfinding around cultural venues in the
city.
d)      
Ensure rural areas are
included in cultural planning.
e)      
Use MK60 as a platform for building community and
neighbourhood cultural events.
f)        
Consider engagement with supplementary schools and
home-schooled children.
g)       
Ensure sustainable sources of funding and strengthen
links with the private and business sectors.
h)      
Encourage digitisation of the living archive
records.
i)         
Emphasise effective communication
strategies.
j)         
Takes account of the wider implications around the
Ox-Cam Arc, Universal Studios and the
new events venue and how these could impact Milton
Keynes.

3.            
That the Director of Planning and Placemaking
be asked to ensure that there is a
public consultation phase on the draft strategy prior to final
approval.

4.            
That officers are
encouraged to ensure ongoing liaison between culture,
economic development, and sports teams to support the linked
working in this area.
topline: The council has approved recommendations for the Creative and Cultural Strategy in Milton Keynes, addressing issues of diversity, infrastructure, funding, and community engagement.

content:
The Head of Economic Development highlighted that the focus
of the report was on the Council Plan commitments and Corporate
Peer Review recommendations that were relevant to the economic
development remit.
The Chair noted that he had received an email from a member
of the public and officers indicated that they would provide a
written response to the queries raised as well as to the questions
submitted in advance by Councillor Muzammil.
A
member of the committee congratulated the team on their work on
Smart City, Digital Tech & Creative Industries and queried the
collaboration with Starship Robots. They also expressed concerns
about the devolution footprint that the Council was pursuing and
cited lost funding opportunities, Growth Hub funding longevity,
skills pipeline and collaboration with South Midlands Authority
partners. Officers indicated that in relation to robotics there was
the RoboPass licensing project for public realm robotics aiming at
creating a replicable framework for other authorities which
Starship was engaged in.  Regarding
devolution it was noted that the footprint was a political matter
but indicated ongoing close work with partners on the South
Midlands Growth Hub and Careers Hub, Connect to Work and Get South
Midlands Working programmes. It was further noted that mayoral
authorities received agreed settlements, while non?mayoral areas
compete for remaining funds, and that this had been raised with
Government that areas seeking devolution should not be
disadvantaged.
A
member queried whether foreign delegations produced tangible inward
investment; how to support local businesses amid low business
confidence; requested sight of the Future High Street report and
assurance of business engagement in the Local Growth
Plan.  Officers noted that the impacts
of delegation visits were often indirect and long?term. With regard
to business confidence officers noted that while national trends
were downward, locally Milton Keynes can project confidence through
City Plan 2050 and skills pipeline partnerships. It was further
noted that there was ongoing engagement with the Federation of
Small Businesses and Chamber of Commerce. It was indicated that the
Future High Street report could be made available, MK vacancy rates
compared positively to national averages and that the COVID
response funds had been passported directly to high streets in
addition to the Council’s £3m programme. Regarding the
Local Growth Plan, a sector strengths analysis had been
commissioned and business engagement would follow.
A
member reported several recent closures on local high streets and
asked whether remaining funding could be directed to struggling
areas. Officers clarified the £3m COVID programme had all
been spent by 31 March 2024, and that additional Government funds
had been directly passed to high streets and Centre MK. Further it
was reaffirmed that ongoing case?by?case support was open to
businesses reporting difficulties.
A
member queried: what public outcomes the Smart City projects
delivered beyond metrics; how the Council would handle community
engagement for RoboPass on Redways; whether a visitor economy
action plan for Universal Studios was in development; and about
Tech Week/AI festival economic outcomes and inclusion. Officers
explained that the Smart City Strategy now had a published action
plan; RoboPass would test public services such as cleansing and
that public engagement was being built into the process. On
Universal, a planning announcement was anticipated and described
initial cross?authority working with Bedford on economy, skills,
housing market impacts, transport/infrastructure, and short?term
accommodation and that the Council would work internally on other
matters. Regarding Tech Week/AI Festival, officers were proud of
the Council?led first year and hoped for increasing private?sector
leadership going forward and emphasised the inclusion of women in
tech, neurodiversity and broader inclusion and that stronger school
engagement was planned for 2026.
A
ward councillor present highlighted the strategic role of East West
Rail as the connective thread for Universal Studios, predicted
leisure becoming a leading employment sector and encouraged Member
briefing papers to include parishes given the significance of these
developments.
A
member queried rate relief uptake and whether all eligible
high?street businesses received it. 
Officers indicated that rates relief was automatically applied by
the Business Rates team.
The Chair queried whether there was any scenario planning
in case Universal Studios did not progress or underperformed.
Officers considered Universal’s case was realistic but agreed
even “smaller?scale” success would be transformative
and that formal scenario work would follow planning
consent.
The Chair asked about the potential for imaginative
MK–Bedford transport connections. Officers noted that the
Council was exploring a mass rapid transit solution that was
sustainable and high?capacity.
It was queried as to whether Bedford or other adjourning
authorities might resist collaboration to protect their own
interests. Officers believed all areas would benefit but that
Milton Keynes as the closest city with a strong night?time offer,
would naturally absorb much demand and reaffirmed working with
others to maximise shared benefits.
It was queried as to whether the Council was aware how many
businesses were closing and officers explained that official
closure/opening data came via annual sources, while the team used
ongoing engagement to identify issues in real time.
A
committee member noted that there was a need to monitor hotel
inflation prices so Milton Keynes remained affordable to residents
and requested an update on a university presence in the city.
Officers confirmed joint meetings with neighbouring authorities on
hotel demand and that MK’s Hoteliers Association welcomed
Universal given current occupancy rate challenges. The current
higher?education presence was outlined as well as ongoing talks
with the Open University and new conversations with prospective
university providers.
A
member observed that Milton Keynes’ night?time economy needed
improvement and asked for an update on any plans for this and on
the casino. Officers advised on the forthcoming events venue which
would be the largest immediate uplift, stimulating growth and
complementing the Theatre and existing nightlife. With regard to
the casino, officers noted that they would ask the relevant team to
provide the committee with an update.
RESOLVED:

1.            
That the Director of Planning and Placemaking be
asked to circulate to the Committee the ‘Future High
Streets’ report.

2.            
The Committee noted and encouraged the proactive
engagement of the Economic Development team with the Federation of
Small Businesses and the Chamber of Commerce.

3.            
The Committee requested that the Director of
Planning and Placemaking ensure collaborative work with adjoining
authorities to maximise benefits from the proposed Universal
Studios development. This should include scenario planning,
consideration of innovative transport solutions for travel between
Milton Keynes and the park, and continue to monitor the impact of
hotel prices on affordability.

4.            
The Committee welcomed the current MK:U and
Cranfield University provision and encouraged continued work to
secure a city-centre university presence.

5.            
The Committee welcomed news of the new city-centre
events centre.

6.            
The Committee requested that the Director of
Customer and Community Services provide the Committee with an
update on the current position regarding the
Casino.

7.            
The Committee requested that the Director of
Planning and Placemaking ask officers to respond in writing to the
questions submitted in advance by Councillor Muzammil and from the
member of the public.

content:
The Head
of Partnerships and Resilience introduced the MK Together Annual
Safeguarding Report to the Committee. She highlighted that the
publication of an Annual Safeguarding Report is a statutory
requirement and the 2024/25 report had been published in September
following agreement by the Safeguarding Partnership.
The
Committee heard that the Safeguarding Partnership was chaired by
Chief Superintendent Emma Baillie and considered the work of
multiple agencies in relation to safeguarding matters. The Head of
Partnerships and Resilience advised the Committee that the
Partnership had a new independent scrutineer this year which had
provided an opportunity to have a new perspective on the work of
the Partnership and they were pleased to have received feedback
that the relationships within the Partnership were mature and that
there was strong leadership.
Members of
the Committee asked questions about the lack of data within the
report and the ability to measure outcomes. The Director of Adult
Services responded that the Council does hold a lot of safeguarding
data but it was not usual practice to include this information in
an Annual Safeguarding Report. The Head of Partnerships and
Resilience added that the Partnership had an assurance group which
considered the sharing of data amongst partners but would not be
involved in individual decisions.
In
response to a further question relating to the data the Council
held the Director of Adult Services confirmed that, where that data
indicates an issue that the Partnership needs to be aware if it
will be brought to their attention and gave an example relating to
a significant increase in safeguarding referrals from the emergency
services being discussed at the Partnership.
Members of
the Committee expressed that they felt there was a need for
relevant, proportionate data to allow them to explore the topic
further in the future and discussed the possibility of requesting
an accompanying data report when considering safeguarding items in
the future.
RESOLVED
–

1.     
That the Committee note the
report.

2.     
That consideration be given to
requesting an accompanying data report for any future agenda items
relating to safeguarding.
topline: The Health, Housing & Adults Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve the MK Together Annual Safeguarding Report and consider requesting an accompanying data report for future safeguarding agenda items.

content:
Following
a request from the Committee, Public Health, Adult Services and
Environment and Property produced reports based on selected key
performance indicators (KPIs).
The Deputy
Director of Public Health introduced the report on the 3 selected
Public Health KPIs relating to the healthy weight and alcohol
support services. She highlighted that the healthy weight service
for both adults and children used to be provided by an external
provider and had recently been brought back in house. The Committee
heard that there had been a period of transition from the previous
service which had temporarily impacted on the availability of data
as the data available wasn’t reliable.
In
relation to the alcohol support services the Committee heard that
preliminary figures for Q2 showed improved performance exceeding
targets. The Deputy Director of Public Health highlighted that
there had been concerns around incomplete data being provided by a
subcontractor which was improving but would continue to impact data
until March 2026 as the indicator used 12-month rolling
data.
Members of
the Committee raised concerns about the management of contractors
and expressed that the provision of data should be part of the
contractual obligations for external contractors. There were
further comments about whether it would be possible to commence the
new service ahead of the closure of the previous contract to ensure
continuity of service for residents. The Deputy Director of Public
Health responded that as the staff were subject to a Transfer of
Undertakings (Protection of Employment) this would not have been
possible in this instance.
The
Director of Adult Services then presented the selected KPIs from
Adult Services. The Committee heard that there had been an error in
the performance report relating to allocations assessments and that
the current average time for processing a housing application was
80 days, which was below the target of 33 days. The Director of
Adult Services indicated that there had been an increase in the
number of applications following the reopening of the housing
register and the team was working overtime to help clear the
backlog. The Committee noted that this was only the beginning of a
long process and that significantly speeding up the processing of
applications would not necessarily mean that people were housed
much faster as demand was still significantly higher than
supply.
In
relation to temporary accommodation, it was noted that families
requiring larger homes often experienced the longest stays in
temporary accommodation as there was less suitable permanent
accommodation for them to move on to, with 3- and 4-bedroom
properties being particularly difficult to source.
Following
a comment from the Committee in relation to downsizing incentives,
the Director of Adult Services advised that there had been 11
requests between April and September 2025 and that the incentive
scheme was being reviewed. She added that people are often
reluctant to leave their properties for several reasons such as
emotional ties and proximity to work or schools.
Following
a query in relation to rough sleepers, the Director of Adult
Services advised that the council was required to undertake a
single-night assessment of rough sleeping to form part of national
statistics. She acknowledged that the number of rough sleepers
counted on that single evening was not a direct comparison to the
figures that the Rough Sleepers Team were aware of and that many
people who sleep rough often have quite changeable circumstances
which may mean they are on and off the streets.
The
Committee were pleased to hear there were no older people awaiting
admission to a care home and that there were no indications that
anyone had not been admitted to a care home where they required
that level of support.
In
relation to the Environment and Property directorate the Committee
discussed the progress of the condition surveys of council homes.
The Assistant Director of Housing Maintenance, Investment &
Corporate Health & Safety advised that just under 400 surveys
had been conducted at the time of the meeting and that there had
been issues with tenants not keeping appointments. She acknowledged
the importance of the relationship with tenants and the need for
clear explanations and reassurance that the condition surveys are
purely to ensure that the property is in good order. The Committee
asked to be kept informed when the data from these surveys had been
processed.
The
Committee also received information in relation to the processing
of void properties. It was noted that as more data was collected
about the condition of properties and tenancies ahead of them
becoming void the spend on voids had reduced, although there were
still some properties returned in poorer condition which therefore
necessitated a higher expenditure. In response to a question from a
member of the Committee the Director of Environment and Property
stated that there were occasions that it was found that a tenant
had conducted unauthorised works during
their tenancy and a view would have to be taken as to whether these
works could be retained or the property would need to be returned
to its previous state. He added that the completion of any works
without permission was a breach of the tenancy agreement.
 
RESOLVED
–
That the
Committee note the contents of the reports relating to selected key
performance indicators within the remit of the
Committee.
topline: The Health, Housing & Adults Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve recommendations based on key performance indicators for various services and housing issues.

content:
The Head
of Homelessness and Tenancy Services introduced the report,
highlighting that the resident engagement strategy set out the
council’s vision for building strong relationships with
residents and had been co-produced with them. She expressed that
the approach to the strategy was to ensure transparency and
accountability for residents of council properties and demonstrate
a desire to listen to and act on their feedback.
The Head
of Housing Operations added that this was an important piece of
work to create a formalised Resident
Engagement Strategy built out of the work of the Resident
Engagement Board which included officers and residents. She advised
the Committee that the Resident Engagement Board had been
fundamental to setting the workstreams and areas of focus that were
included in the strategy.
Two of the
residents who formed part of the Resident Engagement Programme
Board were in attendance at the meeting
and advised the Committee of their personal experience of being
part of the Board. They explained that the Programme Board had
looked at the annual report and the progress made against it and
advised that they felt there was now more personal and engaged
communication than previously.
The
Committee heard that three defined workstreams had been created to
address specific parts of the resident experience where it was felt
improvements could be made. These were building trust, my
neighbourhood and my repairs. It was
noted that each workstream had a dedicated lead and an associated
working group.
Members of
the Committee expressed concerns at the number of residents
involved in the programme board,
stating that they felt many more residents would need to be
involved in order for this to be
reflective of all residents of council owned properties. Officers
responded that the number of residents involved had increased
throughout the process and there was an ambition to include more
residents in future. They highlighted that being part of the
programme board was a significant
commitment in terms of time and not all
residents would have the free time to do this. The Head of Housing
Operations added that the strategy included a three-level
engagement framework for residents where they could commit to other
roles such as that of block champion and that housing managers had
publicised their availability for
drop-in sessions and walkabouts as a means of providing greater
access for residents.
A
discussion was held regarding housing repairs and the difficulties
residents faced when making complaints about repairs. Members of
the Committee expressed that they felt residents needed more
ability to contact the repairs contractor directly.
Concerns
were raised in relation to the lack of baseline data and targets
within the Strategy and the inability to look back on the strategy
in future years and see how successful it had been. The Head of Housing Operations clarified
that the intention was for the residents to assist in the setting
of the targets for the service and that the Resident and
Officers’ Reflection Board would receive regular updates on
progress against those targets. Members of the Committee expressed
that they would like to consider how the Committee could work with
the Reflection Board in the future.
A Member
of the Committee raised that the strategy made no specific
references to leaseholders and older people and that it was
important to ensure that the strategy was comprehensive and
addressed the needs of all residents. One of the residents
present added that she felt it was
important that not just the council but also contractors understood
the needs of residents fully, particularly things such as health
conditions, where this might have an impact on their ability to
access services.
A question
was posed about any penalties that had been imposed on council
contractors as a result of poor service
to residents. The Director of Environment and Property responded
that officers were aware that people’s individual
circumstances could have an impact on their experience of the
services provided by the council and its contractors and that the
council would need to examine evidence to understand what
improvements could be made.
The
Committee were in agreement that they
supported the co-production of strategies with residents and
highlighted that they felt residents should be involved in the
process of creating any strategies and implementing service
roll-outs at the earliest possible stage
to ensure openness and transparency. 
RESOLVED
–
1.     
That the Committee note the
contents of the report and the Draft Resident Engagement
Strategy.
2.     
That the Cabinet Member for
Housing be asked to amend the draft strategy prior to adoption to
include clear targets, measurements and timeframes as well as
details of how these will be monitored.
3.     
That the Committee expresses
support for the co-production of strategies and service
roll-outs with residents and their
inclusion in the process at the earliest possible stage.
4.     
That, prior to any decision on
the adoption of the Strategy, consideration be given by the Cabinet
Member for Housing to how diverse communities can be represented on
the programme board.
5.     
That the Committee requests to
be informed of any targets included within the Strategy and to
receive a future update on progress.
topline: The Health, Housing & Adults Scrutiny Committee has decided to approve the Draft Resident Engagement Strategy with requests for clearer targets and diverse community representation.
