content:
RESOLVED:

1.      That this Council welcomes
the publication of the New Town Taskforce report which names Milton
Keynes as one of the twelve potential sites for the next generation
of new towns.

2.      That this Council
notes:

a)           
Being a new town may provide the opportunity to
ensure that as the city grows, we attract even greater levels of
investment in affordable homes, public transport, health facilities
and other infrastructure required to deliver successful
communities.

b)           
The opportunity to engage proactively with
government on shaping the future plans
for Milton Keynes and delivery of the level of affordable housing
the city needs.

3.     
This Council believes that, in order to
build resident confidence and ensure that new development
contributes positively to Milton Keynes, this Council:

a)           
Supports efforts for the Council to continue acting
as the local planning authority and retain appropriate planning
committee powers.

b)           
Recognises the value of the Council continuing to
play a key role in preparing development briefs to help shape
thriving and sustainable communities.

c)            
Supports that planning for any new development must
take into account the likely long-term
traffic flows to help to minimise impacts on existing
communities.

d)           
Supports the principle of adoptable standards, with
appropriate arrangements and funding for future transfer of public
assets to the Council.

e)           
Believes that effective tenant and homeowner
representation must be included in the governance of management
companies to ensure residents have an active role in how their
communities are managed.
4.                
That this Council asks:

a)           
All councillors to support working with government
to ensure that the views of local people are reflected in how the
proposals are progressed and that local people retain a strong role
in future decision-making.

b)           
The executive to ensure proper engagement on the
benefits that a new town could bring to our residents, businesses
and our economy.

c)            
The executive and senior officers to keep
councillors, stakeholders and the local community fully informed,
as appropriate, on how discussions are progressing.
topline: The Council has decided to support the potential designation of Milton Keynes as a new town, with a focus on affordable housing, public transport, and community engagement.

content:
RESOLVED:

1.      Milton Keynes City Council
believes that bullying is unacceptable in any form and in any
setting – whether in schools, workplaces, online or public
life – and is a damaging behaviour that causes profound
negative effects on the mental health and long-term well-being of
young people. The issue of bullying is particularly significant in
school and educational settings.

2.      Milton Keynes City Council
notes:

a)           
That bullying is now increasingly prevalent through
digital platforms, enabling bullies to harass victims from
anywhere, creating new challenges for intervention.

b)           
That while the act of bullying is harmful, the
behaviour often comes from a complex set of underlying issues,
which must also be addressed.

3.      Milton Keynes City Council
therefore resolves to:

a)      Ask the Cabinet Member for
Children and Young People to work with officers to encourage all
local schools and educational settings to have robust anti-bullying
policies with appropriate reporting tools, enforcement and help for
victims and proper behavioural change support for
perpetrators.

b)      To ask the Chief Executive
to write to our 3 local MPs asking for backing for this Council's
campaign and to call for an increase in resources dedicated to
schools to help tackle and prevent bullying, particularly in the
growing digital landscape.
topline: The Milton Keynes City Council has decided to address the issue of bullying in school and educational settings by implementing robust anti-bullying policies and calling for increased resources dedicated to schools.

1.      That this Council notes

tackling inequalities in ageing, and that nationally over 100 local

2.      That this Council

That the Centre for Ageing Better is working to make
all our workplaces, homes and communities inclusive of older
people, as well as building an Age-Friendly Movement so that
society sees ageing in a more positive and realistic
way.

b)           
That if this work is carried out effectively, more
of the residents of Milton Keynes can experience good health,
financial security and be treated fairly and with respect as we
grow older.

3.            
That this council therefore asks the executive to
officially register to become an Age-friendly Community[2] demonstrating the
Council’s commitment to all our citizens of whatever age and
acknowledging that the needs of older populations must be
recognised and understood.

4.            
That this Council notes Leeds City Council’s
Age Friendly Leeds Strategy and Action Plan 2025-2030, which shows
how working together with local organisations, health services, and
older residents can make a real difference to people’s lives,
by improving housing, transport, health, and community involvement
for older people.

5.            
That this Council therefore:

a)      Asks the Executive to look
at the Leeds approach and other good examples when developing
Milton Keynes’ own age friendly plans.

b)      Encourages close working
with local community and voluntary groups, health partners, and
older residents to create a local action plan that fits Milton
Keynes.

c)      Supports the idea that
“age friendly” means welcoming and inclusive for
everyone, helping to build stronger links between different
generations and reduce loneliness across the city.
topline: The Council has decided to officially register to become an Age-friendly Community, in line with the Centre for Ageing Better's initiatives.

content:
The
Committee received the latest information relating to the Medium
Term Financial Strategy and one-off budget pressures and began
their scrutiny of the pressures and their associated business
cases.
Adult
Services
The
Director of Adult Services was in attendance to respond to queries
relating to pressures within the service area. Following a question
from the Committee she confirmed that there had not been any
significant changes in the financial position of the service in the
last 6 months.
P26-2L
Older People
The
Committee expressed concern that the figure associated with
increased demand for older people was low comparative to other
areas of Adult Services. The Director of Adult Services advised
that this was modelled on the current year’s expenditure and
that demand and expenditure in other areas of the Adult Services
budget are higher. 
P26-1L
Learning Disabilities
It was
noted that the majority of users of the learning disabilities
service were transitioning from Children’s Services but there
had also been increased demand from users who were moving out of
their parent’s homes into supported accommodation for
increased independence. The Committee queried why the rate of
increase in the budget pressure appeared to outweigh the projected
demographic growth. 
OP26-3N
Community Alarm
A question
was asked in relation to the one-off budget pressure associated
with community alarms. The Director of Adult Services advised that
this was related to the monthly cost of a SIM card following the
digitalisation of the community alarm service for residents in
sheltered accommodation who were automatically connected. She
confirmed that this was listed as one-off pressure as a
consultation would be conducted with the residents. The Committee
asked to be advised whether any pressures had been associated with
the community alarm service in previous years. 
Children’s Services
The Lead
Finance Manager for Children’s Services gave a presentation
on the budget pressures associated with Children’s Services.
She highlighted that the biggest driver of demand was the number of
looked after children which had increased dramatically over the
past two years but was now starting to stabilise. The Committee
heard that as a result of the growth in numbers, along with
children presenting with more complex needs, more children had been
placed in residential care which was the most expensive form of
provision.
It was
noted that the current 2026/27 draft budget had been set using the
projected number of looked after children and the expected
proportion of children in each placement type. The Committee heard
that due to the costs associated with one child being placed in
residential care being on average £400,000 a year the actual
expenditure in this area was particularly volatile.
When
presented with the figures broken down by provision type the
Committee asked the reason why such a small increase in expenditure
on residential provision was predicted given the evidence of
previous years. The Assistant Director for Children and Families
responded that the numbers of looked after children were reducing
and also that the practice change to Child First had also
contributed. The Assistant Director also highlighted that the
number of Public Law Outline Processes had decreased by 33% which
would suggest that fewer children would become looked
after.
A further
question was asked in relation to contingencies. The Director of
Finance and Resources responded that there was a robust contingency
figure built into the base budget. The Director of Children’s
Services added that the Department for Education actions to bring
down the cost of private sector residential care homes were also
helpful in avoiding exponential increases in the cost of external
placements.
The
Committee also raised a question in relation to efforts to increase
the amount of available internal fostering placements. The
Assistant Director highlighted that there was a Changing Because We
Have To project focusing on diversifying foster care being led by
the Director of Finance and Resources. She also expressed that
following increased advertisements there had been an increase in
interest in becoming a foster carer but that unfortunately not all
the people coming forwards were eligible and there hadn’t
been as many conversions as hoped for.
The
Director of Finance and Resources elaborated that this was a
national issue as external fostering agencies paid more money to
foster carers. He added that the project was particularly
considering how they could target certain groups who would be more
likely to be able to foster and how to increase sufficiency. The
Director of Children’s Services added that sometimes current
foster carers were lost due to them assuming full parental
responsibilities for the child that they were fostering so a
placement was being lost but for a good reason.
Members of
the Committee expressed that the process of applying to become a
foster carer was very long and asked what could be done about it.
The Director of Children’s Services responded that the
process was heavily restricted by legislation which did extend the
time it took although the service was considering how assessment
processes could be expedited.
Other
Services
A Member
of the Committee raised a question in relation to the closure of
the current Household Waste Recycling Centres and whether there
should be an associated financial pressure in the
budget.
P26-16L
Planning Income and P26-17L Land Charge Income
The
Committee heard that pressures previously included in the budget
had been reduced as planning and land charge income had
increased.
P26-28L
Planning Academy Continuation
The
Assistant Director of Finance confirmed that this was a reduction
of a previous pressure in the budget as some planners had qualified
and further qualified planners had been recruited.
OP26-10N
CMK Events Fund
The
Committee requested a breakdown of expenditure of this
fund.
The
Committee also discussed that it may be necessary to consider
contingencies within the budget at a later date.
RESOLVED
–
That:

1.     
the public and press be
excluded from the meeting by virtue of Paragraph 3 (Information
relating to the Financial or Business Affairs of the Authority) of
Part I of Schedule 12a of the Local Government Act 1972,
for any discussion relating to the exempt briefing
note on pages 47 – 49 of the agenda pack.

2.     
the information contained
within the Budget Pressures Reports be noted.
topline: The council has decided to approve recommendations on budget pressures in Adult Services, Children's Services, and other areas.

content:
RESOLVED:

1.      That this
Council:

a)      recognises the vital importance of early detection
in saving lives from prostate cancer, which is now the most common
cancer in men in the UK;

b)      notes with concern that,
unlike breast cancer screening for women, there is no comparable
national screening programme for
prostate cancer, despite evidence that early identification
significantly improves treatment outcomes;

c)      believes that this unequal
provision leaves men, particularly those most at risk,
disadvantaged and unnecessarily vulnerable, and
therefore;

d)      calls on the Cabinet and
Chief Executive to write to the Secretary of State for Health and
Social Care urging the Government to support calls for a routine,
accessible prostate cancer screening programme; and

e)      further asks that the
Council works with local NHS partners, charities and community
groups to raise awareness of prostate cancer risks and the
importance of early testing until such a programme is in place.
topline: The Council has decided to call for a national screening programme for prostate cancer to address disparities in early detection.

content:
RESOLVED:

1.      That this
Council:

a)      Strongly welcomes the
passage of the Bus Services (No.2) Bill 2024 which is in its final
stages of parliamentary approval.

b)      Notes the New Towns
Taskforce report recently published by the Ministry of Housing,
Communities, and Local Government which identifies Milton Keynes as
a new town location and highlights the potential for significant
Government investment in a future Mass Rapid Transit
system.

c)      Recognises that while the
proposed Mass Rapid Transit system will, in the long-term, provide
a transformational step in addressing Milton Keynes' transport
needs, residents cannot afford to wait years for reliable bus
services. The city urgently needs a bus service that is affordable,
accessible, and reliable now.

d)      Requests the Administration,
working with officers to bring forward an integrated proposal for a
Milton Keynes City Council backed bus service that can meet the
city's immediate transport needs and operate effectively alongside
the new plans for the Mass Rapid Transit system once it is fully
developed and operational.

e)      Recognises that delivering a
Council-run bus service would be a complex and specialist
undertaking, and that the Council may not currently have the full
technical or managerial capacity required to do so. Therefore,
request that the proposal in d) includes any additional resource
that would be required to fund and recruit any necessary external
specialist expertise and operational oversight required to design,
implement, manage and monitor an effective, value for money service
for residents, that is both credible and sustainable.
topline: The Council has decided to develop a Council-backed bus service to address immediate transport needs in Milton Keynes, alongside plans for a future Mass Rapid Transit system.

content:
RESOLVED:

1.      Milton Keynes City Council notes
misleading claims placed into the public domain that
Buckinghamshire Fire Authority has made any proposals to reduce
service levels in Milton Keynes and is dismayed that early
discussions between officers with employee representatives have
been falsely portrayed as anything other than initial discussions
over potential options for service reform.

2.      That this Council would not support any
future proposals to reduce service capacity at Broughton and West
Ashland fire stations.
3.            
That fire service
appliances require trained firefighters to crew them in order to be
operational.
4.            
The Council requests
Buckinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service provide details of any
proposals to change fire and rescue capacity in relation to new
employment models and alternative, more agile firefighting
vehicles.
5.            
The Council asks the
Cabinet Member for Community Safety to write to the Chief Fire
Officer to set out why Milton Keynes City Council would not support
any future proposal to reduce operational capacity at West Ashland
and Broughton fire stations.
6.            
The response should
highlight the assurances given to Milton Keynes residents regarding
fire cover by the former Chief Fire Officer when the
Conservativemembers of the Conservative controlled Buckinghamshire
and Milton Keynes Fire Authority voted to close Great Holm and
Bletchley Fire Stations, and why retaining and enhancing the
current operational capacity is important, to reflect the proposed
growth of the city.
7.            
That the Council
condemns the misinformation that local Conservative councillors in
Milton Keynes and MPs in Buckinghamshire have been circulating
which has unnecessarily concerned the public, and for misleading
statements suggesting that initial discussions at an officer level
are formal proposals that are in some way the equivalent of the
disgraceful decision by the Conservative members of the
Conservative controlled Buckinghamshire and Milton Keynes Fire
Authority to close Great Holm and Bletchley Fire Stations which
reduced fire and rescue capacity and appliances in Milton
Keynes.
8.            
While under
Conservative control, Buckinghamshire Fire and Rescue Service was
given two inadequate inspection reports by HMICFRS, which
consistently criticised the failure of the then Conservative-led
authority to review resource levels in some areas of
Buckinghamshire that are not actually genuinely operational, and
that instigating hysterical and fundamentally untrue campaigns on
matters of public safety is dangerous and disingenuous political
opportunism with no basis in fact.
topline: The Council has decided to reject any proposals to reduce operational capacity at Broughton and West Ashland fire stations amidst political controversy and misinformation.
